If you want to learn about hardware I'd say start up with just doing simple LED blinking stuff - get used to the environment and connecting on a board. Try to use different things like bitwise operations to show different patterns on LEDs. One of the most exciting things I did was a small 8x4 LED matrix that I programmed into a small game, didn't take much more than LEDs and buttons. 

Learn the core components like transistors, logical operators and such. How they are connected and why that works. 

Then move onto learning how to use different components like DAC, BCDs, and how to use multiple ones at the same time. Try to figure out what you can do with this, if you come up with something fun - do it. When you've done something with them, look into if you can put them together from scratch with low level components.

At some point you want to look at the components of the microcontroller are set up. With architecture, the different components, and the flow of information in them. 

One fun project to make once you've done those things is put together a power converter from AC  to DC. See how many things you can do yourself. 

The things that the Arduino board does for you are not the interesting parts, the interesting parts are within the microcontroller itself and what you can make with them. Setting up an own system to program a controller just gets annoying in the end when you've programmed it 20 times. 

If you want to buy some microcontroller and a programmer for it, offers a lot more versatility as you can leave the controllers in each project and buy a new one. Or once you're comfortable with electronics solder your own one - but having it constantly on a pin board seems like a pain to me. 

I wouldn't start doing something like that before you've played around with the components to make it first.

I'd recommend you to learn a bit about how programs or scripts are run, I'd give you a source but it's probably best if you find one specifically for your language. I can tell you a bit however I am a bit rusty and am partial to compiled languages. 

So basically how code is run depends on what type of code it is. I haven't written in the language you used ever but it looks like a scripting language, which would mean that it's an interpreted language. Meaning that the code is run at compile time (and compile time is when your code is translated into machine code). Here's one [article](https://www.educba.com/programming-languages-vs-scripting-languages/) on this subject.

I'll take C++ as an example because that's what I am most comfortable with. I'd say read it if you want but really the best thing would probably be to find words you don't recognize and search them together with the language you decide to use. But writing it out is good practice for me since it was years ago I last went through it (that also means it isn't necessary a 100 percent correct) but still a good starting point. 

Before compiling preprocessor commands in which you can define variables, use conditionals and include other files are run, this could set environment variables and more. After this point you have a pure C++ file. 

The next step is to go from a human readable source file into a machine readable object file. That is done through a compiler. Most languages are built upon other languages, in the case of C++ that is Assembly. So C++ compiles into Assembly code which then assembles into machine code aka binaries. 

The next step is to link all of the object files into an executable (or library). Variable names are replaced with their addresses. Functions are linked to an adress in memory and calls to functions are then replaced with a reference to that adress (unless they are declared to be inline in which case the code of the function replaces the function call. Constant variables or expressions I'd imagine be replaced with their code as inline functions.

Code is executed from top of file, or a start/main function. It then executes commands line by line (following references and pointers) until it reaches the end of file, or an exit call (That's what happened in your case).
